title: A subtropical cyclopoid copepod can increase body size and maintain exoskeleton formation under ocean acidification and warming
content:
Abstract

Evidence is mounting that future marine ecosystems will be disrupted by ocean acidification and warming due to increasing concentrations of atmospheric CO2 and other greenhouse gases. One of the major concerns is the potential impact on zooplankton communities, which may influence the stability of food webs and energy flow in oceans. Since copepods are the most dominant group of zooplankton, we examined whether the subtropical cyclopoid copepod, Apocyclops royi, can optimize the performance of vital physiological processes, including food consumption, body growth, reproductive output, and exoskeleton formation, under ocean acidification (pH 7.8) and warming (ambient +4°C) across four generations. Compared to control conditions (pH 8.1, 22°C), we found that copepods consumed more food under ocean warming, possibly leading to the observed increase in fecundity. Body growth was also facilitated by ocean warming, which may be attributed to the increased chymotrypsin activity that can promote molting. While oxidative stress, represented by lipid peroxidation, was induced by ocean warming, copepods could counter this stress by boosting antioxidant capacity. Synthesis of astaxanthin in copepod exoskeletons was retarded by ocean acidification, but this adverse effect was mitigated by ocean warming. Overall, ocean warming exerted a stronger effect than ocean acidification on the health of copepods, while the transgenerational effect was not discernible. Our findings suggest that some copepod species may consume more food to obtain extra energy that supports various physiological processes under ocean acidification and warming so that their health, populations, and ecological contributions could be maintained in a future warmer, high-CO2 world.
